extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, and natural history (naturalists/classifiers)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for forming natural classifications (Orders, Families, Genera) and a systematic taxonomy of fallacies—how to recognise, classify, and avoid common modes of bad reasoning. Useful for those constructing scientific classifications or evaluating the sufficiency of evidence and arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural affinity as primary principle of division
rubrics_metrics.description: The main principle of division must of course be natural affinity; the classes formed must be natural groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Groups (classes, orders, families, genera) should be formed on the basis of natural affinities rather than arbitrary distinctions. This is the foundational requirement for any scientific classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary divisions grounded on degrees of the main phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary divisions must be grounded not on all distinctions indiscriminately, but on those which correspond to variations in the degree of the main phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break the series at points where variation in intensity of the principal phenomenon (e.g., Sensation, Thought, Voluntary Motion in animals) is accompanied by conspicuous changes in miscellaneous properties. Example: breakpoints where Mammalia ends, fishes are separated from insects, insects from mollusca, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juxtaposition of primary natural groups along a definite scale
rubrics_metrics.description: When primary natural groups are so formed, they will compose the series by mere juxtaposition, each corresponding to a definite portion of the scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure primary groups map to contiguous, determinate regions of the overall scale rather than being redistributed; each group should occupy a coherent interval in the hierarchical series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivision of families to reflect relative position in the general scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Each family should, if possible, be so subdivided, that one portion of it shall stand higher and the other lower, though of course contiguous, in the general scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer subdivisions within families that preserve a local ordering (higher/lower) contiguous in the broader series; only resort to subdivisions based on characters unrelated to the main phenomenon when such an ordering is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form groups according to the most important characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the principal phenomenon transcends all other properties, groups should be formed according to the most important characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give decisive weight to characters connected with the principal phenomenon of interest; avoid forming groups based on secondary or irrelevant traits (e.g., Cuvier's overemphasis on mode of alimentation is criticized). Use the most significant characters to guard against inappropriate clustering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid undue reference to secondary or irrelevant characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not constitute groups so as to place in the same group things which ought to occupy different points of the general scale by giving undue reference to less relevant properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of classifications that rely heavily on features only indirectly connected to the primary phenomenon (example: alimentation), since such features may appear at many levels of the scale and mislead arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of natural arrangement principles beyond biology
rubrics_metrics.description: The principles of natural arrangement are applicable to all cases in which various parts of any extensive subject are to be brought into mental coordination (e.g., arrangement of a code of laws).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat classification tasks in art, business, or law with the same scientific conditions used in natural history: seek natural groups and a coherent series aligned with the principal organizing phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include fallacies as part of a complete philosophy of reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete philosophy of reasoning ought to comprise the theory of bad as well as of good reasoning; enumerate the varieties of apparent evidence which are not real evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teaching or practising reasoning, explicitly identify common modes of bad reasoning and apparent evidence mistaken for genuine evidence; this catalogue is essential to avoid accepting error for truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish casual errors from systematic fallacies
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude mere accidental lapses (hurry, inattention) from the analysis of fallacies; focus on modes of performing reasoning that are fundamentally wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expend philosophical classification on simple carelessness; instead, analyse and classify persistent or principled errors that mislead reasoning even when attention is given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise moral vs intellectual sources of error
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources of erroneous opinion are twofold: moral (indifference to truth, bias) and intellectual; moral causes act indirectly by perverting intellectual cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When diagnosing error, separate the moral motivations (bias, wishful thinking) from the intellectual malfunction (admitting insufficient evidence). Strengthening intellectual disciplines (rigorous methods) mitigates errors that moral causes exploit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguard against bad reasoning by cultivating habit and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The only complete safeguard against reasoning ill, is the habit of reasoning well; familiarity with the principles of correct reasoning, and practice in applying those principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasise training, repeated practice, and internalisation of correct methods rather than only theoretical admonitions; habitual application reduces susceptibility to fallacies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify fallacies by cause or by the kind of evidence they simulate
rubrics_metrics.description: Fallacies may be arranged according to the cause which makes things appear evidentiary, or according to the particular kind of evidence which they simulate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both axes (origin of the illusion and the type of genuine argument it imitates) to organise fallacies for clearer diagnosis and remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: Fallacies of Simple Inspection (à priori) vs Fallacies of Inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Fallacies of Simple Inspection (à priori) arise when a proposition is believed or presumed without extrinsic evidence; Fallacies of Inference arise from erroneous conclusions from supposed evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether an asserted proposition rests on no external evidence/presumption (à priori) or on misapplied premises; different remedies apply (expose presumption vs test premises).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Confusion (lack of fixity of conceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fallacies of Confusion arise when premises are not conceived with due clearness or fixity, leading to substitution of different premises or conclusions during argument (includes language vagueness/ambiguity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure clear, fixed conceptions of premises throughout reasoning; inspect for equivocation, vagueness, or unconscious substitution of terms or concepts as a source of error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate fallacies simulating induction vs deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent evidence may simulate either simple induction (particular facts) or deduction (foregone generalizations); fallacies should be classified accordingly into inductive or deductive types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing an error, determine whether it purports to be an induction from facts or a deduction from general principles to apply appropriate critical tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Observation (inductive fallacies from erroneous facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive fallacies where the facts on which the induction proceeds are erroneous (mal-observation, non-observation, or inference from intermediate marks that do not prove the intended fact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify the accuracy and completeness of observed facts, check for mistaken marks or proxies, and guard against drawing conclusions from misobserved or unobserved data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Generalization (inductive fallacies from correct facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases where the facts are correct but the generalization drawn from them is not warranted by those facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overgeneralization; assess whether the available instances legitimately support the breadth of the claimed general proposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Deduction / Ratiocination (vicious syllogisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductive fallacies in which the premises (though possibly true) do not support the conclusion; cases of vicious argumentation guarded against by rules of the syllogism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check logical form and whether the conclusion follows necessarily from premises; apply syllogistic rules and tests for validity to expose these fallacies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate both truth and conclusiveness of premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent evidence may be false in itself, or true but inconclusive; fallacies may arise from either defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When testing an argument, independently evaluate (a) the truth of premises and (b) whether, if true, they suffice to warrant the conclusion; both dimensions must be satisfied for legitimate inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief in evidentiary relation requires belief in habitual conjunction
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot regard one fact as evidentiary of another unless we believe the two are always, or in the majority of cases, conjoined (as antecedent, consequent, or concomitant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand reliable generalisation of co-occurrence before treating any fact as evidence for another; check the empirical frequency or causal necessity of the conjunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerate fallacies by specifying properties that make facts appear evidentiary
rubrics_metrics.description: An enumeration of fallacies consists in a specification of those properties in facts, and those peculiarities in our mode of considering them, which give rise to mistaken beliefs that they are evidentiary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When compiling or using a taxonomy of errors, focus on the characteristic properties of facts or cognitive habits that create false impressions of evidence, so remedies can target those properties/habits.
